papers.title_in_file: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics Undergraduates' Knowledge and Interest in Quantum Careers: Barriers and Opportunities to Building a Diverse Quantum Workforce
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, methods (participants, data analysis), findings section A, discussion, limitations, start of recommendations. Interview-theme sections skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A mixed-methods survey and group-interview study of STEM undergraduates at one U.S. university on their knowledge of and interest in quantum careers.

assertions.value: The authors report that most surveyed STEM undergraduates knew very little about quantum, and that 63% rated their interest in a quantum career at 3.0 or higher on a 5-point scale.
quotes: We found that most of the students know very little about quantum.
with 63% rating their interest a 3.0 or higher on a continuous 5-point scale
assertions.certainty_reason: One survey at one university; self-reported, non-random sample.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says 186 students were surveyed while the Participants section says 185; the paper does not reconcile the two.

assertions.value: The authors report that across all majors men (n = 68, M = 3.256) reported greater interest in a quantum career than women (n = 49, M = 2.608), t(115) = 3.201, p=0.002.
quotes: Across all majors, students who identified as men (n = 68, M = 3.256, SD = 1.01) reported a greater interest in pursuing a career in quantum than students who identified as women (n = 49, M = 2.608, SD = 1.17), t(115) = 3.201, p=0.002.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-institution survey t-test.

assertions.value: The authors report that when only computer science and physical science majors were compared, there was no statistically significant difference between women (n = 32, M = 3.000) and men (n = 62, M = 3.30) in interest in a quantum career, t(92) = 1.289, p = 0.100.
quotes: we found no statistically significant difference between women (n = 32, M = 3.000, SD = 0.20) and men (n = 62, M = 3.30, SD = 0.13) in their interest in a quantum career, t(92) = 1.289, p = 0.100.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-institution survey t-test; a non-significant result with modest samples.
assertions.reader_inference: Not significant is not the same as no difference; the sample sizes are small.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results come from a single institution and so may not be applicable in all settings.
quotes: the results are from a single institution so the results may not be applicable in all settings.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own Limitations section, p.13.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Normalizing Flows for Anomaly Detection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, preliminaries, method overview, experiments section (setup, metrics, datasets), summary. Proof-level detail of the architecture search skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A method that finds quantum-gate sequences acting as normalizing flows and uses them for semi-supervised anomaly detection on the iris and wine datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that their optimized quantum normalizing flow models show competitive anomaly-detection performance against isolation forest, local outlier factor and one-class SVM baselines.
quotes: Our proposed models show competitive performance for anomaly detection compared to classical methods
The optimized architectures show competitive performance despite being fully implementable on a quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on two small toy datasets from one study; AUROC values are in Fig. 5, not quoted here.
assertions.reader_inference: Competitive is the authors' wording; no figure is quoted, so the size of any gap is not captured.

assertions.value: The authors state that the models train on normal data only, and that for the iris dataset they train on 50% of the points of one class and test on the remaining points plus a second class.
quotes: In this work we assume that only normal data is available during training.
We select 50% of data points from one class (e.g. setosa) for training and use the remaining datapoints, as well as a second class (e.g. virginica) for testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that they assume the system is not subject to decoherence or other external noise.
quotes: We further assume that the system is not subject to decoherence or other external noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated assumption, Section II A.
assertions.reader_inference: The results are therefore noise-free simulation results, not hardware results.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiments (statistical comparison, qiskit comparison, hardware runs), summary and discussion. Method derivations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: Three transpilation-style methods (stochastic search, database lookup, random-forest guided) that shorten quantum circuits for restricted gate sets while preserving the unitary.

assertions.value: The authors report average computation times of 199 seconds for the random-search variant V1-RS, 55 seconds with database lookup, and 38 seconds for the random-forest variant V3, over 100 randomly generated circuits of length 100.
assertions.anchor: Experiments, statistical comparison, Fig. 7 and Table II
quotes: For this experiment we randomly generated 100 different starting circuits of length 100 and reduced the circuit to a target size.
Whereas V1-RS requires in average 199 seconds, already the database lookup reduces the compute time to nearly a quarter (55 seconds).
The variant V3 making use of the random forest brings the average computation time down to 38 seconds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical timing from one study; the authors exclude graph build and classifier training time.

assertions.value: The authors report that on IBM:Brisbane a random two-qubit circuit of length 40 was transpiled to a circuit length of 156, while its reduced equivalent of length 8 was transpiled to 34 circuit blocks.
quotes: In the next experiment we generated a random two qubit quantum circuit of length 40 (long) and reduced it to a quantum length of 8 (short), keeping the implemented unitary intact.
On the IBM:Brisbane, the long circuit has been transpiled to a circuit length of 156, whereas the short circuit has been transpiled to just 34 circuit blocks.
assertions.certainty_reason: One circuit pair on two IBM chips; the authors call the 2-qubit case nearly trivial.

assertions.value: The authors state that their method is significantly slower than the qiskit transpilers, is only useful when a highly efficient circuit block is reused several times, and is best suited to very long circuits with a smaller number of qubits.
assertions.anchor: Experiments p.9; Summary and Discussion p.11
quotes: It should be noted that our method is significantly slower than the qiskit transpilers and our approach is only useful when a highly efficient circuit block is required and reused several times in a larger context.
our algorithm is best suited for very long circuits with a smaller amount of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section V.

papers.title_in_file: Stochastic Neural Networks for Quantum Devices
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, classification experiment (iris), Hopfield section, generative/Grover section, conclusion. RBM, autoencoder and CNN sections skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A gate-based quantum circuit model of stochastic artificial neurons, trained with the Kiefer-Wolfowitz algorithm and simulated annealing, with a Grover-oracle generative use.

assertions.value: The authors report that in one run on the iris dataset their algorithm classified all test samples correctly, and that gradient descent shows large variance with a low average score due to local minima.
assertions.anchor: Experiments, shallow networks, Fig. 10 and Table I
quotes: In this run, the algorithm could perfectly classify all test samples.
Please note the large variance of gradient descent, which results in a low average score due to local minima during optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single reported run on a toy dataset; the Table I averages are not quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is one run, not an average. The paper states gradient descent was run without augmentation or dropout.

assertions.value: The authors state that their model itself does not provide a direct quantum advantage, and that models at the scale of current state-of-the-art neural networks will only become practical on future fault-tolerant large-scale quantum devices.
quotes: A second important aspect is that even though our model itself does not provide a direct quantum advantage, in combination with known approaches indicating a quantum advantage it can provide powerful new methods

As the amount of available qubits is limited, and the qubits suffer from decoherence, models at a similar scale will only become practically available on possible future fault-tolerant large scale quantum devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limits, Introduction p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experiments are based on binary input patterns, and claim the framework can easily be extended to more general qubit states.
quotes: Our experiments are based on binary input patterns, but the framework can be easily extended to more general qubit states, as clarified later.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the scope of its own experiments, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The extension to general qubit states is asserted, not shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that sampling the circuit combining a frozen trained network with a Grover search leads to a highly-efficient generative model.
assertions.anchor: Section IV G, Generative Neural Network, p.16
quotes: Thus, sampling this circuit leads to a highly-efficient generative model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim backed by histograms of tiny 2x2 patterns; no efficiency comparison quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: Efficiency is asserted for toy pattern sizes only; no resource count or classical comparison is quoted.

papers.title_in_file: Sequential Hamiltonian Assembly: Enhancing the training of combinatorial optimization problems on quantum computers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, evaluation setup, solution quality (6.2), Max-Cut results, conclusion. Background sections and strategy details skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: An extended study of Sequential Hamiltonian Assembly, which trains parameterized quantum circuits by building the loss from local Hamiltonian terms, evaluated by simulation on graph coloring and Max-Cut.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Max-Cut problem SHA performed better than the comparison methods, with improvements of up to 43,89 % for the VQE and 29,08 % for the Layer-VQE.
quotes: In our new experiments we have shown that SHA still performs better than comparative methods when applied onto the Max-Cut problem with improvements of up to 43,89 % for the VQE and 29,08 % for the Layer-VQE.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results on small graphs from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract states the same figures as mean accuracy; the paper's Max-Cut text states that the median was constant at 3 except for one setting.

assertions.value: The authors report that SHA8 showed a 17.58% better mean accuracy than layerwise learning and 5.12% better than Layer-VQE, while the QAOA baseline still performed significantly better than all VQE-based approaches in raw accuracy.
quotes: Specifically, SHA8 shows a 17.58% better mean accuracy than LL and 5.12% better than L-VQE, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.
However, the QAOA baseline still performs significantly better than all VQE-based approaches in terms of raw accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results from one study at low layer depth.
assertions.reader_inference: The QAOA baseline beat every VQE-based method in raw accuracy, so SHA does not win overall in this experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Max-Cut results should be further validated on larger problem instances, and that future work should investigate scalability for deeper parameterized circuits.
quotes: This results should be further validated on larger problem instances.
Future work should investigate scalability for deeper PQCs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limits, Section 6.2 and Section 7.

papers.title_in_file: Automated Quantum Algorithm Design using a Domain-Specific Language
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results, discussion, start of methods. Appendix motif descriptions skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: An evolutionary-search method over a domain-specific language of circuit motifs that learns n-qubit versions of known quantum algorithms from small examples.

assertions.value: The authors report that their method rediscovered the quantum Fourier transform, the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm and Grover's search, learning the general implementation from example circuits of at most 5 qubits.
quotes: Remarkably, we were able to learn the general implementation of each algorithm by considering examples of circuits containing at most 5-qubits.
We successfully rediscover the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm, and Grover's search
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on three known algorithms.
assertions.reader_inference: All three targets are known algorithms; no new algorithm was found.

assertions.value: The authors report 50 experiments for each combination of task and search space size, and state that the method can plausibly run on a personal computer with a 90% chance of success within two days in most cases.
quotes: A total of 50 experiments were performed for each combination of task and search space size
with a 90% chance of success within two days in most cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' summary of experiments in one study; per-configuration rates are in Table I and not quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists per-configuration success rates, some well below 1.00 for larger search spaces; the 90% figure is the authors' summary, and the in most cases wording is theirs.

assertions.value: The authors state that rediscovering these algorithms validates the approach and outlines how it could be used to discover a new algorithm given a well-posed task.
quotes: validating our approach and outlining how it could be used to discover a new algorithm given a well-posed task.
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking author claim; no new algorithm is shown in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Discovery of a new algorithm is not demonstrated.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 2 start, results (Table 2, Fig. 4 text), discussion. Methods, appendices and baseline details skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: AlphaTensor-Quantum, a deep reinforcement learning method that minimizes T-count of quantum circuits by symmetric tensor decomposition, with support for gadgets.

assertions.value: The authors report that AlphaTensor-Quantum outperforms the existing methods for T-count optimization on a set of arithmetic benchmarks, even when compared without making use of gadgets.
quotes: AlphaTensor-Quantum outperforms the existing methods for T-count optimization on a set of arithmetic benchmarks (even when compared without making use of gadgets).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical benchmark result from one study; figures are in Table 2, not quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The Table 2 caption says it matches or outperforms the baselines for circuits that were not split into sub-circuits, which is narrower than the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors report that for multiplication in finite fields AlphaTensor-Quantum finds an efficient quantum algorithm with the same complexity as the classical Karatsuba's method.
quotes: AlphaTensor-Quantum finds an efficient quantum algorithm with the same complexity as the classical Karatsuba's method
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical discovery by one method; no proof of optimality beyond selected decompositions.

assertions.value: The authors state that AlphaTensor-Quantum does not come with optimality guarantees, and that its gains come at the cost of increased computational complexity (around 8 hours to optimize the addition circuits of Cuccaro et al.) and loss of optimality due to extra compilation steps.
quotes: although AlphaTensor-Quantum does not come with optimality guarantees

this comes at the cost of increased computational complexity (e.g., it took around 8 hours to optimize the addition circuits of Cuccaro et al. [43]) and loss of optimality due to extra compilation steps
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limits, Discussion p.14.

assertions.value: The authors state that, like most prior works, they consider the T-count as the sole metric of complexity of a quantum circuit.
quotes: Like most of these works, and for the reasons laid out before, we consider the T-count as the sole metric of complexity of a quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own optimization target, Introduction p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Results say nothing about circuit depth or other costs.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Kernel Estimation With Neutral Atoms For Supervised Classification: A Gate-Based Approach
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, kernel estimation procedure, results, discussion, conclusion. Pulse-level gate derivations skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A gate-model method for quantum kernel estimation on neutral-atom devices, built from laser-pulse-derived gates and evaluated by simulation on a 3-feature toy dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report a mean test accuracy of 75% for the quantum-kernel SVM and a mean accuracy of 65% for an SVC with a radial basis function kernel.
quotes: a mean accuracy of 75% is obtained, calculated using the test kernel matrix previously estimated.
obtaining a mean accuracy of 65%, which is sensibly lower than the one obtained with the quantum approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated result on a small artificial dataset from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors say the dataset was designed to make high accuracy possible with this method, so the comparison with the RBF kernel does not show an advantage on real data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sequences could not be run on real hardware and that the simulation was restricted to only 3 features because of the computational effort required by QuTip.
quotes: Due to the impossibility of running the sequences on a real hardware, the simulation was restricted to the case of only N = 3 features because of the computational effort required by QuTip when the number of qubits increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper also states the sequence takes almost 80 microseconds while current Pasqal devices support about 10 microseconds, so the circuit exceeds present hardware limits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dataset was designed to make a high classification accuracy possible with the method and that it is just an artificial example for theoretical purposes.
quotes: it is evident that it was designed to make a high classification accuracy possible using the classification method illustrated in this paper and in [5], and it is evident that it is just an artificial example for theoretical purposes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit, Section IV.
